name: Department of the Taoiseach
request_description:
My request relates to the DPMA allowance. On Feb 1, 2023 the then Taoiseach, Leo Varadkar, took Leaders' Questions and addressed issues related to the withholding of the DPMA allowance from certain individuals in care.  https://www.oireachtas.ie/en/debates/debate/dail/2023-02-01/10/
He said:
In 1996, the allowance was renamed the disability allowance and responsibility for it was transferred to the Department of Social, Community and Family Affairs, as it was called at the time.
Since 2007, it has been paid in full to people with disabilities living in long-term care, so this matter was resolved 15 years ago. However, the question that arose in 2009 was whether there should have been retrospection and back pay. It is an historical issue, a legacy issue, but to me it does appear different from the nursing homes charges issue. It appears different in substance because the legal advice is different and the legal advice and position became clearer after the High Court ruling. It is something we are going to look into over the next week or two and respond to further.
And the legal advice on the DPMA was that the State did not have a leg to stand on.
Over the course of the next few days comments from other ministers discussed potential restitution and other options.
I seek: All correspondence and documents on the issue regarding the assessment, discussion or resolution of this issue. This should include any details on measures proposed or tabled to address this matter and any memo that went to the Taoiseach's office on this issue.
For the avoidance of doubt, the purpose of this request is to establish what actions were taken or considered to address this. My request can be limited to any document created or circulated after January 28, 2023.
The request is focused on the DPMA issue and not the similar nursing home issue that was also discussed in the debate.

Please also be advised that I am not confining myself in this request to representations made by elected public representatives, but include any representations made. Please further note that I am including any references to where a serving member of the judiciary wrote on behalf of themselves to seek promotion. While I am happy for personal information such as home addresses and home telephone numbers to be redacted, I request that identifying names be disclosed. To assist with my request, I refer you to a previous decision from the Information Commissioner, the Sunday Times and Department of Justice (Case No. 100263), in which the applicant sought similar records as in this request. The Decision Maker stated: Applying this general public interest in transparency to the records at issue here, it is clear that the public interest is served where the process of judicial appointments is made as transparent as possible. It is not just the fact that judges are paid from public funds but more important perhaps is the fact that they are entrusted, on behalf of the people, with independent and far-reaching powers. Furthermore, there is the reality that the process of judicial appointments lacks innate transparency and that, outside of the limited scope of FOI, there is very little by way of effective transparency mechanisms.

• Documentation of consultations with external experts specializing in childhood trauma or psychological harm when designing the scheme.
2. Residency Requirement Criteria (180-Day Rule)
• Minutes, reports, or correspondence discussing the establishment of the 180-day residency requirement for scheme eligibility.
• Assessments evaluating the psychological, emotional, and financial impact of this residency rule on survivors who were excluded due to shorter stays.

3. Institutional Reclassification & Exclusion of Survivors
• A list of institutions that were initially classified as Mother and Baby Homes or Children’s Homes but were later reclassified as Nursing Homes or other facilities.

• Any legal or policy advice given to the government on this matter.
4. Consultation Process & Survivor Feedback
• Records of consultations held with survivors or advocacy groups regarding the 180-day requirement and the exclusion of certain institutions.
• Documentation showing how survivor feedback was considered in the final decision-making process.
5. Additional Questions on Scheme Development
• Minutes of all meetings held by the Interdepartmental Group concerning the development of the Restorative Recognition Scheme from its establishment to the present date.
• Correspondence (emails, letters, or memos) exchanged between your department and other government bodies regarding the Restorative Recognition Scheme.
• Reports, proposals, or cost analyses prepared by or submitted to the IDG relating to the development and implementation of the scheme.
• Details of any financial allocations or budgets assigned to the scheme by your department, including any projected costs and payments made to date.
• Any legal advice or assessments received by your department regarding the exclusion of certain survivors from the scheme.
• Internal communications, policy discussions, or decisions regarding the refusal to conduct an excavation of Sean Ross Abbey or other Mother and Baby Home sites.
• A list of individuals, organisations, or external consultants who were involved in advising or assisting with the scheme.
6. Costing and Financial Valuation of Trauma in the Restorative Recognition Scheme
• Records outlining how the financial compensation amounts were determined for survivors in the scheme.
• Any economic assessments, cost-benefit analyses, or internal discussions on how to put a monetary value on trauma and suffering experienced by survivors.
• Minutes, reports, or correspondence regarding the decision-making process for setting the payment amounts based on length of stay.
• Any external consultants or research studies referenced when deciding on the financial compensation structure.
